q: Why is isinstance(True, int) a trap in validation?
options: It’s True, so a careless check accepts true as 1

q: What must a permission check do when it can’t complete?
How do you keep a user’s value out of SQL syntax?
What’s the safe way to run a command with a user’s file name?
options: subprocess.run with a list, no shell, and – before the name

q: Which escaping protects a value inside an HTML attribute?
options: html.escape with quote=True, inside a quoted attribute

q: What is SSRF?
explain: Refuse private, loopback and link-local addresses.
options: Making the server request an internal address chosen by the attacker

q: Where should production secrets live?
options: In the environment, from a secret manager

q: A key was pushed to a public repository. What first?
What does pip install –require-hashes protect against?
explain: Every file must match its hash.
options: A different file installed under a locked name and version

q: What is dependency confusion?
options: A public package hijacking an internal package’s name

q: Why store passwords with PBKDF2, scrypt or Argon2 rather than SHA-256?
explain: SHA-256 is too fast for passwords.
options: They’re slow and salted, so guessing is expensive

q: What must never repeat with the same encryption key?
explain: Reuse leaks the XOR of the plaintexts.

q: Which key makes a digital signature?
explain: Anyone can verify with the public key.

q: What does this print?
explain: fullmatch rejects extra characters; x is too short.
code:
import re
print([n for n in ["ok_1", "ok_1;", "x"] if re.fullmatch(r"\w{2,10}", n)])

q: Why keep the rules in a module with no web or database code?
options: The rules can be tested alone and shared by every layer

q: Why is a status change POST /tickets/{id}/transitions rather than PATCH of the status field?
options: A transition has its own rules and history, so it’s a resource of its own

q: Why is assigning a ticket a PUT?
options: Setting the same assignee twice has the same effect as once: PUT is idempotent

q: What should validation do with a field the client wasn’t meant to send, such as status?
options: Refuse the request, naming the field

q: Why collect every validation problem rather than stopping at the first?
options: The client can fix everything in one go

q: What does writing the state machine as a table make possible?
explain: Data can be checked; scattered ifs can’t.
options: One check in the code, documentation from the same data, and automatic checks of the table itself

q: Why answer 404 when a customer asks for someone else’s ticket?
explain: Don’t leak what users may not see.
options: So the API doesn’t confirm that the ticket exists

q: Why should an unknown action name raise an error in allowed()?
options: So a typo in the code is found at once instead of silently denying (or allowing)

q: Which status means “readable, but invalid”?
explain: 400 is for requests that can’t be read at all.

q: What does this print?
explain: Only one move from open is open to agents.
code:
TRANSITIONS = {"open": {"in_progress": {"agent"}}, "in_progress": {}}
print([s for s in ("open", "in_progress") if "agent" in TRANSITIONS["open"].get(s, set())])

q: Why repeat the allowed statuses as a CHECK constraint in the database?
options: So nothing can store an invalid status, even code that bypasses the domain rules

q: What must you do for SQLite to enforce foreign keys?
options: PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON on each connection

q: Why does each migration run in its own transaction?
explain: A half-applied migration is the worst state to be in.
options: So it’s applied completely or not at all, with its record

q: What should happen if the database’s version is higher than the code knows?
explain: Old code on a new schema can corrupt data.

q: Why does create_user raise ValueError instead of letting sqlite3.IntegrityError escape?
explain: Translate errors at the layer boundary.
options: So the layers above don’t depend on the database library

q: How does asking for limit + 1 rows help pagination?
options: If the extra row comes back, there’s another page, without a second query

q: What stops two agents overwriting each other’s status changes?
options: UPDATE … WHERE id = ? AND status = ? with the status they saw, and a conflict if no row changed

q: Why is the events row written in the same transaction as the change?
options: So the history can never disagree with the data

q: What does SCAN tickets in a query plan mean?
explain: SEARCH … USING INDEX is what you want for filtered queries.

q: What does this print?
explain: Start with every key at zero, then update.

q: Why make create_app take the clock and the log function as parameters?
explain: Inject what you need to control.
options: Tests can control time (to expire tokens) and read what was logged

q: Why raise ApiError instead of returning an error response?
explain: One place decides what errors look like.
options: Helpers can stop the request from anywhere, and one handler formats every error

q: What should the 500 handler send for an unexpected exception?
options: A generic message and an incident id, with the details only in the log

q: Why does /readyz check the migrations?
explain: Ready means able to do the job.
options: So traffic isn’t sent to an instance whose database isn’t ready

q: Why is the sign-up endpoint only for customers?
explain: Never let a request choose its own privileges.
options: Staff accounts must be created by admins, never by a public form

q: Why check an unknown email against a dummy hash at login?
options: So unknown emails take as long as real ones, and timing doesn’t reveal which accounts exist

q: How does the list endpoint stop a customer seeing others’ tickets?
explain: Never let the client choose its own scope.
options: The web layer adds the customer’s own id to the query itself
It hides them in the HTML

q: Which status for a customer editing a ticket an agent has started on?
explain: The request conflicts with the ticket’s current state.

q: Why filter internal notes in the query rather than in the response?
explain: Data you never load can’t leak.
options: So a customer’s response can never contain them, whatever happens later in the code

explain: 600 seconds after the token was issued.
code:
from datetime import datetime, timezone
print(datetime.fromtimestamp(1800000000 + 600, timezone.utc).strftime("%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"))

q: How do you know a test suite would catch a bug?
explain: A suite that passes on broken code would have let the bug through.
options: Break the code on purpose and check that a test fails (mutation testing)

q: Where do bugs in validation usually hide?
explain: Test both sides of every limit.
options: At the edges: the shortest allowed value and the one just outside

q: Why write a permission test’s expected answers by hand rather than computing them from PERMISSIONS?
explain: The test is an independent statement of the rules.
options: A test that reads the table it checks would pass whatever the table said

q: What do two parametrize decorators on one test do?
options: Run it for every combination of their values

q: Why give every API test a fresh app and database?
explain: Fixtures build a new one for each test.
options: So tests can’t affect each other through leftover data

q: How can a test move time forward to expire a token?
options: Share a clock fixture with the client fixture and change it

q: Why run CI on pull requests as well as pushes?
explain: A red cross stops the merge.
options: To catch problems before they’re merged

q: Why pin actions to a version rather than @main?
options: A moving branch can change under you, including to something malicious

q: Why report routes that never succeeded in tests?
explain: Test the happy path and the refusals.
options: A route tested only with refusals has never had its main job tested

q: Why check every setting at start-up?
explain: Fail fast, with every problem listed.
options: A missing or bad value is found when it’s deployed, not at 3 a.m. on the first request that needs it

q: Why log the request path but not the query string?
explain: Logs are copied and kept for years.
options: Query strings can hold tokens and personal data

q: Why check an incoming X-Request-ID before using it?
options: It’s untrusted input that ends up in logs and headers

q: Why use time.perf_counter for durations?
explain: The wall clock can be adjusted mid-request.
options: It’s more precise and never jumps like the wall clock

q: Why copy requirements.txt and install before copying the code?
explain: Order layers from least to most often changed.
options: So Docker reuses the cached install layer when only the code changed

q: Why not put SECRET_KEY in an ENV line of the Dockerfile?
options: It’s stored in the image’s layers, readable by anyone who can pull the image

q: Why can’t a single release rename a column?
explain: Expand and contract over several releases.
options: The old code, still running during the release, would lose the column

q: Why does adding a NOT NULL column without a default break the old code?
explain: Add it nullable, or with a default.
options: The old code’s INSERTs don’t mention the column, so they all fail

q: A release removes a response field. Which part of the version changes?
explain: Removing a field is a breaking change.

code:
major, minor, patch = (int(x) for x in "2.9.14".split("."))
print(f"{major}.{minor + 1}.0")

q: Why does the helpdesk keep its rules in a module with no web or database code?
options: The rules are written once, tested alone and shared by every layer

q: Which bug lets two agents overwrite each other’s status changes?
options: An UPDATE without the expected-status condition

q: Why does cursor pagination use id > after rather than id >= after?
explain: The cursor is the last item already seen.
options: Otherwise each page repeats the last item of the page before

q: Why must a webhook URL be checked against private and link-local addresses?
explain: Check every address the name resolves to.
options: Otherwise anyone who can register a webhook can make your server call your internal network (SSRF)

q: Why are webhook bodies signed with HMAC?
explain: Shared secret, compared in constant time.
options: So receivers can tell genuine events from forgeries

q: Why does changing a ticket only queue the webhook instead of sending it?
explain: A separate job delivers with retries.
options: The user’s request shouldn’t wait for, or fail because of, someone else’s server

q: Why does each delivery carry an id?
explain: At-least-once delivery means duplicates are possible.
options: So a receiver can ignore a delivery it already handled after a retry

q: Why is the event serialised once, before signing?
explain: Re-serialising could change spacing or key order.
options: The signature must cover exactly the bytes sent

q: Which change can’t be made in one release while the old version keeps running?
explain: Expand and contract over three releases.
